concept.sub_category: Shunyam Saamyasamuccaye (When Samuccaya is Same, It is Zero)

examples.problem_statement: An alternate way of obtaining the RHS is using the rule: ‘Product of the means minus the product of the extremes’

solution.description: Read off the two pairs the problem supplies, (7, 5) and (2, -8), keeping them in that order: the order is what decides which numbers count as means and which as extremes.

solution.operation: Apply the rule: Product of means minus product of extremes
solution.description: Lay the four values out as the single sequence 7, 5, 2, -8. The means are the two inner values, 5 and 2; the extremes are the two outer values, 7 and -8. The rule asks for the product of the means minus the product of the extremes.
Take the first of those two products: multiply the inner values 5 and 2 to get 10.
Now the other product: multiply the outer values 7 and -8. One factor is negative, so the product is negative, -56.

solution.operation: Subtract product of extremes from product of means
solution.description: Subtract the extremes product from the means product. Subtracting -56 is the same as adding 56, so the 10 grows to 66.
Nothing is left to combine, so 66 is the value the rule produces for the right-hand side, confirming the stated answer.

key_reminders: {'point': "Rule: 'Product of the means minus the product of the extremes'."}
{'point': "Verification: 'Thus, the technique can be easily verified !'."}
{'point': "Efficiency claim: 'One can see from the examples mentioned above, the simplicity and straight-forwardness of the Vedic Mathematics approach."}
{'point': "Problems on geometry which take 5-7 steps can be solved mentally just by looking at them!'"}
common_mistakes: Multiplying the extremes as 7 times 8 and losing the minus sign, which turns the last step into 10 - 56 = -46.
Subtracting the means from the extremes instead of the other way round, which flips the answer to -66.
Pairing the numbers as 7 with 2 and 5 with -8, which swaps the means and the extremes.
repair_note: Rewrote all six descriptions so each narrates its own operation: naming the pairs, identifying means and extremes within the sequence 7, 5, 2, -8, the two products, the sign handling in the subtraction, and the closing statement of 66. Kept technique_name 'cross multiplication' and the arrow_matrix scaffold, which matches the crosswise means/extremes pairing the steps use. Added three mistakes tied to the negative factor and the order of subtraction.

examples.problem_statement: Let us suppose I was a member of the audience. My date of birth is 26th June. Then I would have worked out the steps as follows:

solution.description: Turn the birth month into its position in the year. June is the sixth month, so the chain of operations starts from 6.
Double the month number: 2 times 6 is 12. This doubling is what will later have to be undone as part of the subtraction.
Add 5 to the doubled month: 12 plus 5 is 17. That added 5 is carried through the rest of the chain and shows up at the end as 50.
Multiply by 5: 17 times 5 is 85. Combined with the earlier doubling, the month has now been multiplied by 10 and the added 5 by 25.
Multiply by 10, that is, write a zero after 85 to get 850. The two right-hand places are now empty and ready to hold the date.
Drop the day of the month into that empty space: 850 plus 26 is 876. This is the number the volunteer reads out, and it is all the performer hears.

Working backwards from the announced 876, subtract 250. That removes the 200 left by the doubling and the 50 left by the added 5, leaving 626: the 6 on the left is the month, June, and the 26 on the right is the date.

key_reminders: {'point': 'Remember: The trick works because the operations encode the month and date into the final number in a reversible way.'}
{'point': 'Subtract 50 from the last two digits to get the date; subtract 2 from the remaining digits to get the month.'}
{'point': 'Caution: Ensure the participant does not miscount or misstate their birth month or date.'}
{'point': 'Speed Tip: Practice mental subtraction of 50 and 2 quickly to appear instantaneous in revealing the date of birth.'}
common_mistakes: Adding the date before appending the zero, so there is no empty space for it and the decoding fails.
Subtracting only 50 instead of 250, which leaves the month digit two too large.
Reading the leftover 626 as one number instead of splitting it into month 6 and date 26.
repair_note: Replaced the placeholder descriptions ('First operation in the sequence', etc.) with narration of each operation's role in the encoding chain, and rewrote step 7 to explain the subtraction of 250 as undoing the doubling (200) and the added 5 (50), leaving 626 to be read as month 6 and date 26. Note that step 7's operation labels this as the Shunyam Saamyasamuccaye sutra, which it is not; the operation text is frozen and was left untouched. Changed visual_scaffold from arrow_matrix to equation_chain, since the steps are a linear chain of operations with no crosswise structure. Added mistakes for the ordering of the append-zero step and the decoding.

concept.sub_category: Ekadhikena Purvena (One More than the Previous)

solution.operation: Identify the number to be squared: 65
solution.description: The task is 65 squared. What matters is that 65 ends in 5, which is exactly the case the Ekadhikena Purvena sutra handles.

solution.operation: Separate the last digit (5) from the remaining part (6)
solution.description: Split 65 at the final 5: it is 6 tens plus 5, so the part standing in front of the 5 is n = 6.

solution.operation: Apply the Ekadhikena Purvena formula: n × (n+1) followed by 25
solution.description: State the rule for a number written as n followed by 5: the square is n times one more than n, sitting in the hundreds, with 25 written after it.
Carry out the first half of the rule with n = 6: multiply 6 by the next whole number, 7, which gives 42.

solution.operation: Append 25 to the result from step 4
solution.description: Write 25 after that 42, which is the same as 42 hundreds plus 25, giving 4225.

solution.operation: Verify the result using standard multiplication
solution.description: Check the shortcut against ordinary multiplication: expanding (60 + 5) times (60 + 5) gives 3600 plus 600 plus 25, which is 4225, the same answer.
Strip the final 5 off 75 and keep what stands in front of it, n = 7. That is the only piece the first half of the rule needs.
Apply the first half of the rule to n = 7: 7 times the next whole number, 8, is 56, which becomes the leading part of the square.
Apply the second half: the units digit 5 times itself is 25, the two digits that close the answer, so 75 squared is 5625.
Strip the final 5 off 95, leaving n = 9 as the part in front.
Multiply 9 by the next whole number, 10, to get 90, the leading part of the square.
The units digit 5 times itself is 25 as always, written after the 90, so 95 squared is 9025.
The rule does not stop at two-digit numbers. Strip the final 5 off 105 and the part in front is n = 10.
Multiply 10 by the next whole number, 11, to get 110. This whole two-and-a-half digit result is the leading part, not just its last digits.
Close with 5 times 5, which is 25, written straight after 110, so 105 squared is 11025.

key_reminders: {'point': 'Remember, squaring is multiplying a number by itself.'}
{'point': 'In fact, you can mentally calculate the square of a number ending with a 5.'}
{'point': 'Just multiply the non-five numbers with the next number and then multiply the last digits (5 × 5) and add 25 after it.'}
common_mistakes: Multiplying the front part by itself, 6 times 6, instead of by the next number, 6 times 7.
Writing a single 5 after the leading part instead of the full 25, so 75 squared comes out as 565.
Shortening the 110 in the 105 case and writing 1125 instead of 11025.
repair_note: Rewrote every description to narrate its own step, including the three empty ones in the 105 example, and removed the generic copy-paste narration shared by the 75 and 95 examples so each names its own n and its own product. Changed visual_scaffold from arrow_matrix to formula_generalization: the steps state the general rule for a number ending in 5 and then instantiate it four times; no arrows or matrix are used. Deleted the auto-extraction common_mistakes object (trap_id/QC taxonomy filler) and replaced it with three real hazards from these numbers.

concept.technique_name: multiplication of numbers whose last digits add to ten

solution.result: \text{Base} = 10^n \text{ where } n \text{ is number of digits} = 10^2 = 100
solution.description: Notice where the two factors sit: 66 and 64 are both two-digit numbers a little below 100, so 100 is the natural base to describe them against.
Measure each factor against that base: 66 falls 34 short of 100 and 64 falls 36 short.
Rather than carry those deviations any further, set the two factors one above the other, 66 over 64, so the digits can be taken vertically and crosswise.
Start at the right-hand column and multiply the units digits vertically: 6 times 4 is 24. The 4 stays as the units digit of the answer and the 2 is carried left.
Now the crosswise column: 6 times 4 plus 6 times 6 is 24 plus 36, which is 60. Adding the carried 2 makes 62, so 2 is kept and 6 carries further left.
Finish with the left-hand column, the tens digits multiplied vertically: 6 times 6 is 36, and the 6 carried in from the crosswise column lifts it to 42.
Read the columns back from the left: 42 from the tens column, then the 2 kept in the crosswise column, then the 4 from the units column, giving 4224.

solution.operation: Multiply the number 10 by the number that follows it (11)
solution.description: Both factors start with 10 and their last digits, 7 and 3, add to 10, so the shortcut applies: take the shared leading part, 10, and pair it with the next whole number, 11.
Multiply that pair: 10 times 11 is 110, and this becomes the leading part of the product.
Multiply the two last digits: 7 times 3 is 21, written as the closing two digits, so 107 times 103 is 11021.

solution.operation: Multiply the number 9 by the number that follows it (10)
solution.description: Run the same test on 91 and 99: they share the leading digit 9 and their last digits, 1 and 9, add to 10, so pair the 9 with the next whole number, 10.
Multiply the pair: 9 times 10 is 90, the leading part of the product.
Multiply the last digits: 1 times 9 is 9, which has to be written as the two digits 09, so 91 times 99 is 9009.

solution.operation: Multiply the number 5 by the number that follows it (6)
solution.description: 51 and 59 share the leading digit 5 and their last digits add to 10, so pair the 5 with the next whole number, 6.
Multiply the pair: 5 times 6 is 30, which is the leading part of the product.
Multiply the last digits: 1 times 9 is 9, padded out to 09 so it fills two places, giving 3009.

key_reminders: {'point': '(Note: The right hand part should always be filled-in with a two-digit number.'}
{'point': 'Caution: Always ensure both conditions are met — last digits sum to 10 AND remaining digits are the same.'}
common_mistakes: Using the shared leading digit twice, 5 times 5, instead of pairing it with the next number, 5 times 6.
Writing a single 9 for 1 times 9 instead of the two digits 09, which turns 3009 into 309.
Reaching for the shortcut when the last digits do not add to ten or the leading parts differ.
repair_note: Corrected technique_name from 'squaring' to 'multiplication of numbers whose last digits add to ten': no example squares anything, and all four multiply distinct factors sharing a leading part with last digits summing to 10. Rewrote every description to its own operation, including the misattached base claims (the 91 by 99 example was described as base 90 and the 51 by 59 steps carried unrelated talk of the difference-of-squares identity). The first example's steps 1-2 measure deviations from 100 that no later step uses, so the narration says plainly that step 3 sets them aside for the vertical-and-crosswise layout. Kept arrow_matrix, which matches that layout. Deleted the auto-extraction common_mistakes object and wrote three hazards, including the 09 padding.

solution.description: 57 sits just above 50, so write it as the base 50 plus a deviation of 7. Everything that follows runs on that 7.

solution.operation: Apply the Vedic formula for squaring numbers near a base
solution.description: State the rule for numbers in the fifties: the square is 25 plus the deviation on the left, followed by the deviation squared as the last two digits.
Build the left part: add the deviation to 25, so 25 plus 7 is 32.
Build the right part: square the deviation, 7 times 7 is 49, which already fills the two places the right part needs.
Set the two parts side by side, 32 then 49, and read them as one number, 3249.
Check it the long way: (50 + 7) times (50 + 7) is 2500 plus 350 plus 350 plus 49, which is 3249, matching the shortcut.
The units digit of 56 is 6, and for a number in the fifties that units digit is the deviation from 50. Adding it to 25 gives 31, the left part of the square.
Square that same units digit: 6 times 6 is 36, and it already occupies the two places the right part needs.
Write the left part next to the right part, 31 then 36, so 56 squared is 3136.
The units digit of 52 is 2, so the left part is 25 plus 2, which is 27.
Square the units digit: 2 times 2 is 4, and a single digit will not do here, so it is padded to 04 to fill both places.
Join the parts, 27 then 04, giving 2704. The padding zero is what keeps the answer from collapsing to 274.
The units digit of 53 is 3, so the left part is 25 plus 3, which is 28.
Square the units digit: 3 times 3 is 9, padded to 09 so the right part occupies two places.
Join 28 and 09 to read off 2809.

key_reminders: {'point': '• Remember: The RHS must always be represented as a two-digit number.'}
{'point': 'If squaring the units digit yields a single digit, prefix it with a zero (e.g., 4 becomes 04, 9 becomes 09).'}
{'point': '• Note: This technique applies only to numbers between 50 and 60.'}
{'point': '• Speed Tip: This method avoids long multiplication — you only need to add 25 to the units digit and square the units digit, then concatenate.'}
common_mistakes: Writing a one-digit right part, so 52 squared comes out as 274 instead of 2704.
Adding the whole number to 25 instead of just its units digit.
Using the method outside the fifties, where the left part is no longer 25 plus the units digit.
repair_note: The 53 example's three descriptions were pure filler about 'pattern' and 'Urdhva Tiryagbhyam principle' rather than its own arithmetic; rewrote them and every other description to name the deviation, the 25-plus-deviation left part, the squared deviation right part, and the two-digit padding. Changed visual_scaffold from arrow_matrix to formula_generalization, since step 2 states the general rule for the fifties and the later examples instantiate it. Added three mistakes, led by the dropped padding zero in 2704.

examples.problem_statement: Subtract 54.36 from 100 using the Vedic Mathematics rule 'All from 9 and the last from 10.'

solution.operation: Identify the number to be subtracted from 100
solution.description: The subtraction is 100 minus 54.36. Because the number being subtracted from is a power of ten, the sutra can replace the borrowing entirely.

solution.operation: Apply 'All from 9, last from 10' to each digit of 54.36
solution.description: Take the digits of 54.36 in order and subtract each from 9, apart from the very last one, which comes off 10 instead: 5 gives 4, 4 gives 5, 3 gives 6, and the final 6 gives 4.
Write those four results in the same order the digits were taken, 4, 5, 6, 4.
Put the decimal point back where 54.36 carried it, two places from the right, so the digits read 45.64.
Check by adding the two numbers back together: 54.36 plus 45.64 is exactly 100.00, which confirms the complement.

examples.problem_statement: Subtract 3478.2281 from 10000 using the same rule.

solution.result: 9 - digit for all digits except last
solution.description: Take every digit of 3478.2281 except the final one and subtract it from 9: 3, 4, 7, 8, 2, 2 and 8 become 6, 5, 2, 1, 7, 7 and 1.
The final digit is the one that comes off 10 rather than 9: 10 minus 1 is 9. Reading all the digits in order and keeping the decimal point four places from the right gives 6521.7719.

key_reminders: {'point': "Remember: Use the rule 'All from 9 and the last from 10' for quick subtraction from powers of 10."}
{'point': 'Note: In examples (d) and (e), zeros were added to align digits for accurate computation.'}
{'point': 'Caution: Ensure correct digit alignment when padding with zeros.'}
{'point': 'Speed Tip: This technique eliminates borrowing and is faster than traditional subtraction for numbers close to powers of 10.'}
common_mistakes: Subtracting the last digit from 9 as well, which leaves the answer one too small.
Treating the digit just before the decimal point as the last digit instead of the true final digit.
Losing the decimal point: the answer keeps as many decimal places as the number being subtracted.
repair_note: The second example's two descriptions were swapped and generic: 'Handle last digit with the Last from 10 rule' sat on the step that subtracts the other seven digits from 9, and 'Combine results to form final answer' sat on the step doing 10 minus 1.
